name: Treaty with the Delawares, etc., 1803 (Treaty of Fort Wayne)
promises: The boundaries of the Vincennes tract, reserved to the United States at Greeneville in 1795, were fixed, and the United States gave up any claim to lands adjoining it (Articles 1 and 2).
In return for the great salt spring on Saline Creek and up to four miles square around it, the United States would deliver up to 150 bushels of salt every year for the tribes (Article 3).
Tribal members could cross any ferry on the new road toll free in high water (Article 4).
If settlers' lands fell outside the Vincennes lines, the lines would be moved and an equal quantity of land given to the tribes (Article 5).
landTaken: Royce Area 26 (the Vincennes tract, Indiana and Illinois) and Royce Area 47 (the salt spring tract on Saline Creek, Illinois).
compensation: The salt annuity of Article 3. In a 1978 valuation case the Indian Claims Commission counted the Kickapoo share of this salt annuity, which the Kickapoo released in a later treaty, as part of the consideration for that later cession (Dockets 15-D et al., 42 Ind. Cl. Comm. 379).
today: In 1973 the Indian Claims Commission found that no tribe held aboriginal title to Royce Area 26 at the 1795 Greeneville Treaty, and that the boundaries fixed by this treaty were the tribes' acknowledgment of the Vincennes reservation; the related claims in Dockets 13-G, 18-M and 40-F were dismissed (31 Ind. Cl. Comm. 89). That is a ruling against the claimants, not a breach. No claim for Royce Area 47 was found.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says that after signing the first treaty with the new United States in 1778 its ancestors had to keep giving up their lands and moving west, to Ohio, then Indiana, Missouri and Kansas and at last Indian Territory, and that its people understood many early land sales as something closer to leases.

The Tribe says its homelands lie in what are now Indiana, Ohio, Illinois, lower Michigan and lower Wisconsin, that the treaty period was devastating, beginning with the massive cession required at Greenville in 1795, and that settlers kept pressing the Myaamiaki to give up their lands until removal at gunpoint in 1846.

nationVoice.nation: Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma
nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's history says the Peoria, Kaskaskia, Piankeshaw and Wea, united as the Confederated Peoria in 1854, were forced from ancestral lands in Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio, Iowa and Missouri, moved to Missouri, then Kansas, then northeastern Oklahoma, and by 1915 held no tribal land at all.
